problem_statement: The paper frames insurance and actuarial science as the financial problem of modeling and evaluating random risky events across non-life insurance, life insurance, and risk management. It highlights tasks such as pricing premiums, modeling claims and liabilities, mortality forecasting, reinsurance allocation, and portfolio risk optimization.
problem_statement_quotes: Insurance is the financial means helping people to avoid potential loss and to hedge against risk from particular sources [1]. What lies in the core and crux of insurance practice and actuarial science is to model and evaluate random risky events [2].

In the branch of non-life insurance, The central tasks are to price the premiums paid by an individual policyholder, to model the claims for an insurer to afford when an insured event happens, and to estimate the liability considering the Incurred But Not Reported (IBNR) and Reported But Not Paid (RBNP) claims [3].

In contrast, the life insurance branch pays attention to insure life against disability-and-death risk by mortality forecasting [7–9], as well as against live-too-long risk by life annuity pricing [7, 10].

As for the risk management branch, reinsurance and risk indicators are common tools to transfer and quantify the risks, respectively [14]. Consequently, stochastic process catching large claims and risk portfolio optimization are both emphasized when studying the reinsurance problem [7, 11, 15, 16].
classical_baseline: The paper treats Monte-Carlo simulation, regression, neural networks, mortality forecasting models, stochastic-process simulation, multi-period optimization, generalized linear models, the Chain-Ladder model, VaR/cVaR, and mean-variance or stochastic-programming approaches as the classical tools used to address these insurance problems.
classical_baseline_quotes: Therein, Monte-Carlo simulation, regression, and neural network are introduced to solve complicated statistics mathematics and stochastic process problems [4–6].
This can be solved by mortality forecasting models, financial/mortality stochastic processes simulations, and multi-period portfolio optimization [11–13].
The Chain-Ladder Model [49] is a mainstream model used to estimate the IBNR amount.
The Value at Risk (VaR) and conditional Value at Risk (cVaR) are common risk measures in risk management [58].
Techniques such as mean-variance optimization and stochastic programming are commonly used.
classical_difficulty: The paper says the classical difficulty is that insurance and actuarial problems are becoming harder because data are growing rapidly and models are becoming more complex, which demands exponentially more computational resources. It also says realistic data-based calibration and validation are essential, but efficient data encoding remains challenging in the NISQ era.
classical_difficulty_quotes: Nevertheless, the traditional insurance industry and academia are encountering challenges due to the rapidly growing data size and increasingly complex models, which will require exponentially increased computational resources [11].

Similar to other practical applications, quantum algorithms still face significant challenges. For instance, encoding a general distribution into a quantum computer requires the preparation of the corresponding quantum state, which demands exponential resources [90, 91].
Additionally, noise in quantum computers remains a challenge for most quantum algorithms.
business_stakes: The paper says insurance is used to avoid potential loss and hedge against risk, and that effective risk management ensures the stability and profitability of financial institutions. It also notes that better evaluation can support more precise, even online and personalized, risk assessment and can benefit prediction of potential losses.
business_stakes_quotes: Insurance is the financial means helping people to avoid potential loss and to hedge against risk from particular sources [1].

Risk management is a critical aspect of financial and insurance industries, aiming to identify, assess, and prioritize risks followed by coordinated efforts to minimize, monitor, and control the probability or impact of unfortunate events. Effective risk management ensures the stability and profitability of financial institutions.
The risk can be estimated and evaluated more precisely, and such an evaluation process can be even online and personalized, based on quantum computation with Internet and Internet of Things data.
The potential loss can be predicted more early and precisely, benefiting from quantum computational climate predicting, mortality forecasting, and fat-tail events modeling, to name but a few.
extraction_notes: Motivation is explicit and broad; paper is a survey-plus-demonstration on insurance/actuarial science rather than a single narrow finance problem.
